new_statements.quote: [p. 48 n. 5] The stress here is certainly marked in that normal stress in PWG (Ennemor, specifically) is penultimate, when the final syllable is open (Hetzron 1977: 42). It is crucial to note that these converbs are all ending in vowels and yet are stressed. [p. 61] In Ennemor, Hetzron found that the long vowels behave phonologically as a sequence of vowels, evidenced by stress patterns such as /bi'id/ (1977: 36). Unfortunately, the Mesmes data is not consistently marked for stress.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK. File is the 159-page Epson scan of Ahland's May 2004 UTA MA thesis (title page pg-000: 'LANGUAGE DEATH IN MESMES... MICHAEL BRYAN AHLAND... May 2004'); no text layer (extracted text gives 1 char on p. 61), scanned in ocr_thesis/ with printed page = NNN-12. I rendered PDF page 61 (printed p. 48) to an image and read it directly: the footnote reads exactly 'The stress here is certainly marked in that normal stress in PWG (Ennemor, specifically) is penultimate, when the final syllable is open (Hetzron 1977: 42). It is crucial to note that these converbs are all ending in vowels and yet are stressed.' Only difference from the report: it is printed as footnote 25 (the next is 26), n…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Peripheral West Gurage (the subgroup Mesmes belongs to), stress is penultimate when the final syllable is open and falls on a final closed syllable (Hetzron's Inor/Ennemor rule, quoted by Ahland); long vowels count as two vowels. On top of this, a grammatically conditioned final-vowel stress marks the main past and the m-converb (historically a lost suffix -m). Ahland's Mesmes text shows this final grammatical stress on verbs, but his Mesmes data are otherwise 'not consistently marked for stress', so the positional rule for Mesmes itself is inferred from PWG, not observed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Mesmes. Hetzron 1997: 539 (for Inor) describes accentual harmony yielding two stressed syllables (penult + final) and suffixes with their own stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Verb-final vowels marking main past / converb are stressed although open (functionally distinctive stress replacing lost -m); Ahland suggests this 'stress' may underlyingly be compensatory vowel length (p. 125) and that etically it sounds like gemination of the final radical (p. 131). Final -e/-i always stressed per Hetzron 1997 (Inor).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, in connected text (a single Mesmes narrative from the terminal speaker) and comparative wordlists; no citation-form or phrase-level statement. Source is a historical-comparative MA thesis, not a phonological description; no instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand Mesmes source (Ahland 2004, from a single terminal speaker recorded 2001) explicitly says its Mesmes data are 'not consistently marked for stress'. The positional rule (penultimate when final syllable open, final closed syllable stressed) is Hetzron's for Ennemor/Inor (inor1238) and Peripheral West Gurage generally, adopted by Ahland for Mesmes as a PWG language; the only Mesmes-specific observations are the grammatically stressed final vowels on main-past/converb verbs in the text. A catalog entry should be flagged as PWG-inferred, low confidence.

sources.citation: Hetzron, Robert. 1997. Outer South Ethiopic. In R. Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages, 535-549. London: Routledge.
sources.note: p. 539 'Stress': 'In most languages stress, a slight raise of the pitch, is not relevant. Only PWG has a system that is meaningful even for grammar. The following presentation refers to Inor... The basic stress rule is: a final closed syllable is stressed; when the final syllable is open, the stress is penultimate... Final -e, -i are always stressed... Long vowels and diphthongs behave like a sequence of two vowels'; lost suffix -m leaves 'functionally distinctive stress'; accentual-harmony rules give two stressed syllables. Mesmes is not named anywhere in the chapter.
